title: Most harm we do ourselves
hookLine: he argues most suffering comes from what people do to themselves and each other
last: FOR MAIMONIDES, GOD'S CARE FOLLOWS THE TURNED MIND.

cards: A writer once argued that the world holds more evil than good. Count up the pain, the sickness, the grief, he said, and the scale tips the wrong way. Maimonides answered it in the Guide.
He didn't deny that suffering is real. He did something more uncomfortable. He sorted it, kind by kind, and asked where it actually comes from.
And when the sorting was done, the biggest pile wasn't the one blamed on God or on nature.

teach.b: Most harm we do ourselves. From the Guide, part three, chapter twelve. First, the harm of having a body.
Bodies come into being and wear out: illness, injury, the blows of nature. Real, Maimonides says, but the least frequent.

teach.h: WHAT PEOPLE DO TO EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Second, the harm people do to each other: tyranny, violence, war. More common than the first, but still not the largest.
Third, the harm people do to themselves. This, he says, is the most frequent of all. Too much eating, too much drinking, appetites without limits, chasing more than anyone needs.

teach.h: THE WORLD IS NOT ABOUT ME.
teach.b: A person wrecks their health, their peace, their relationships, and then complains about the world.
Some readers find in his discussion that the hunger for luxuries also turns people against each other, so the third kind feeds the second.
He quotes Ecclesiastes: "God made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions." Fourth, why the writer got it wrong.
A person who thinks the whole universe exists for them judges everything by their own small hurts, and so concludes the world is mostly bad.

Step back, and much of what we suffer turns out to be within reach of human choice. This is not a teaching that blames people for their illnesses or their grief. Maimonides keeps the first kind on the list.
It hands back some power: the largest pile is one people can begin to shrink.

how: Jewish teaching on repentance asks a person to examine their own part in what went wrong, and some study Maimonides' account of the three kinds of evil in Guide 3:12 alongside his Laws of Repentance.

games.q: what does “most harm we do ourselves” mean?
o: most pain comes from nature: floods, quakes, storms
most suffering comes from what people do to themselves
harm done by enemies is the largest kind of all

games.q: most harm we do ourselves — tap the pairs.
p: the body wears out, nature strikes
what people do to each other

s: Maimonides says suffering from nature is the most frequent kind
he calls it less frequent than the other two.
he says the harm people do to themselves is the most frequent kind
excess and unlimited appetites, he says, cause the most suffering.
his teaching means people are to blame for every illness
he keeps the harm of having a body on the list. the point is that the largest share is within reach of choice.

games.q: you're Maimonides. a writer argues the world holds more evil than good. how do you answer?
o: agree, and say nothing can be done.
sort suffering by kind, and show most comes from people.
games.why: he sorts it into three kinds and finds the largest is what people do to themselves. the writer, he says, judged the universe by his own hurts.

practice: Think back over the past week to one thing that went wrong, and sort it gently, the way Maimonides would: the body or nature simply happening, something another person did, or some small part that was yours, a habit, an excess, a word.
Don't punish yourself; just find the part that's yours, and one step that would care for it.
If what hurts ever feels like too much to carry, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Most harm we do ourselves. Maimonides' teaching that of the three kinds of suffering, the most frequent is what people bring on themselves, and much of the rest is what they do to each other. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: most harm we do. Held gently, that's hopeful: much of it is within reach. Go gently.
